opus-5.5.text:
Oh, it was humbling, honestly. I came into MIT feeling fairly confident. I'd done a lot of competition math, and I thought, okay, I know how to think about problems. Then I walked into that graduate probability class in my first semester, and within the first couple of lectures I realized the language itself was different. Everyone was talking about measure theory, sigma-algebras, filtrations, martingales, as if these were just the furniture of the room, and I was still trying to figure out where the door was.

I remember sitting there taking notes very fast, writing down symbols I didn't fully understand, telling myself I'd decode them later. Then I'd go back to my dorm and spend hours just trying to reconstruct one proof from lecture. The problem sets were brutal. In competitions there's a trick, a clever insight, and you're done. Here you had to build the machinery slowly and carefully, and if one step wasn't rigorous, the whole thing fell apart.

What helped was swallowing my pride. I went to office hours a lot. I asked questions I was a bit embarrassed to ask, the very basic "what does this notation actually mean" kind. I found a few classmates, some of them grad students, who were kind enough to work through problems with me. I also went back to more foundational textbooks and filled in gaps on my own, almost like running a parallel course for myself.

Looking back, I think that experience taught me something really important: being out of your depth is not a signal that you don't belong. It's just the feeling of learning something genuinely new. If you always feel comfortable, you're probably not growing. That semester changed how I approach hard things. Now when I feel lost, I try to treat it as information about where to go next rather than as a verdict on whether I'm good enough.

fable-5.1.text:
I remember that semester really vividly, because it was the first time I was genuinely out of my depth and couldn't fix it by just working harder.

I'd come in as a freshman, and I got into this graduate probability course. On paper I had the prerequisites. But the first few weeks, I'd sit in lecture and the professor would be talking about measure-theoretic foundations, sigma-algebras, martingales, and I was writing everything down without actually understanding what I was writing. Everyone around me seemed to be nodding along. Later I found out a lot of them were PhD students who had already seen this material once or twice. I didn't know that at the time, so I just assumed I was the slow one.

The first problem set took me something like thirty hours. I was staying in the library until it closed, and I still got problems wrong. That was a very new feeling for me. I'd always been the person who could just push through. And here, pushing through wasn't enough, because the gap wasn't effort, it was that I was missing a whole layer of mathematical maturity underneath.

What actually changed things was a pretty humbling moment. I went to office hours and basically admitted to the TA that I didn't understand the question, not the answer, the question. And instead of being judgmental, he spent an hour going back to the basics with me. He pointed me to a more elementary textbook and said, read the first three chapters this weekend, then come back. That reframed the whole thing for me. It wasn't that I couldn't do it. It was that I was trying to climb a ladder with rungs missing.

So I got a lot more systematic. I started reading ahead, I found a study group, and I stopped pretending in class. If I didn't follow something, I asked. That was uncomfortable, especially as the youngest person in the room, but it was so much more efficient than nodding along and then suffering alone at midnight.

By the end of the semester I did fine. Not spectacularly, but fine. And honestly the grade mattered much less than what I learned about myself, which is that being lost is a state, not an identity. You can be completely out of your depth on a Monday and partially swimming by the next month, as long as you're honest about where you actually are. That lesson has carried over into everything since, including building a company, where you're out of your depth constantly and the only real failure is pretending you're not.

astra-6.text:
It was humbling. I was in my first semester at MIT, taking a graduate probability course, and I felt like I didn’t have the background to keep up. There’s a difference between following an argument while someone explains it and being able to work through it yourself, and that gap felt very real to me.

The challenge was not turning “I don’t understand this yet” into “I’m not capable of understanding this.” I had to be willing to ask basic questions and spend time on things that seemed obvious to other people. Being out of my depth was uncomfortable, but it also meant learning to be a beginner without treating that as a failure.

sol-6.1.text:
It was humbling. I was used to being able to work hard and eventually figure things out, and suddenly I was sitting in a class where I couldn’t follow everything. That was uncomfortable, especially in my first semester, when I was still trying to understand where I fit at MIT.

But it also helped me separate not understanding something yet from not being capable of understanding it. I had to get more comfortable asking basic questions and spending time with ideas that didn’t click immediately. Being out of my depth became less of a verdict on my ability and more of a place where learning could happen.
